newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity closes higher on short-covering.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity closes higher on short-covering.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures closed higher on strong cash market prices and short-covering, market sources said Thursday.
"The strength was really in the front months. Some people got caught short for June and that helped push everything else up," said one trader.
She noted the market remained choppy, with trading volumes still at the relatively thin levels seen for most of the week.

Traders attributed the strength in June cash electricity to unseasonally hot weather in the Southwest, unplanned generating unit outages and transmission de-ratings caused by heavy use of the regional grid system.

With air conditioning demand strong in the Southwest and California, more power was being brought in from the Northwest and Rocky Mountain regions, but the extra volumes caused "loop-flow" problems and some schedules were cut.
Temperatures in parts of the Los Angeles Basin broke above 100 degrees for a second consecutive day, although the weather was expected to moderate starting Friday afternoon.
For the Southwest in general, temperatures were forecast to run about five degrees F above normal through early next week.
In the Pacific Northwest, temperatures were forecast at three to four degrees above normal for the next several days.
NYMEX July Palo Verde (PV) closed at $31.37 per megawatt hour (MWh), up $1.06, but down from a high for the day of $32.50.
August PV closed up $1.10 at $32.80 and September was up 57 cents at $29.36.
The July California-Oregon border (COB) contract settled 71 cents higher at $23.50 per MWh, while August was up 46 cents at $25.99.
September COB gained 21 cents to settle at $24.71.
Estimated trading volumes for the day were not immediately available from NYMEX.
Separately, Arizona Public Service said the 1,221 megawatt (MW) Palo Verde 1 nuclear power unit near Phoenix will be restarted by late Thursday following the reconstruction of a charging pump.
The utility had said it expected to restart the unit Wednesday from a weekend outage to repair a valve leak.
Also, the 1,087 MW Diablo Canyon nuclear power unit remained off line for refueling, and was expected to restart this weekend.

In addition to the Palo Verde and Diablo Canyon nukes, several units were expected to return to service by Monday, including a 750 MW unit at Colstrip in Montana, a 750 MW unit at Four Corners in Arizona, a 550 MW unit at Jim Bridger in Wyoming and a 400 MW unit at the Bonanza plant in Utah.
